titleZh: Cleansing Medicinal Herbs in the Stream on a Spring Day
titleEn: Cleansing Medicinal Herbs in the Stream on a Spring Day
mediumDetail: Handscroll; ink and color on silk
dimensions: Painting only: 36.2 x 132.5 cm (14 1/4 x 52 3/16 in.); Overall in heigh: 38.7 cm (15 1/4 in.)
description: A famous portraitist, Yu Zhiding here depicts the likeness of Shi Shenyi 史申義 (1661–1712), an official and poet. Master Shi, a sickly man, was deeply interested in medicinal science. The opening section of the scroll features a boy washing a fungus in fresh spring water, a basket of medicinal herbs by his side. Other servants carry a fan, a bundle of scrolls, and a cup of tea or hot wine. Master Shi sits in a bamboo grove, surrounded by fields of herbs. Returning swallows, pink peach blossoms, and blooming magnolia indicate spring, whereas the fungus conveys wishes for long life. The spring theme may express the artist’s wish for his friend’s recovery.
note: In the pavilion are some of Shi Shenyi’s scholarly accoutrements: a stack of books, an antique zun 尊 (wine vessel), a brush holder, an ink stone, and a small chime.

titleZh: Sugriva challenges his brother Vali, King of the Forest Dwellers, to a duel, folio 10 from the Kishkindha Kanda (Book of Kishkindha) of a Ramayana (Rama’s Journey)
titleEn: Sugriva challenges his brother Vali, King of the Forest Dwellers, to a duel, folio 10 from the Kishkindha Kanda (Book of Kishkindha) of a Ramayana (Rama’s Journey)
mediumDetail: Gum tempera, ink, and gold on paper
description: In a morally ambiguous scene, the white monkey Sugriva calls to his brother Vali, the rightful king of the forest-dwellers, to emerge from a cave. Behind him, the blue hero Rama hides with his brother and monkey ally Hanuman. Clutching a deadly three-pronged arrow, Rama prepares to slay Vali, so Sugriva will rise as king and be obliged to help locate Rama’s lost wife. Paintings from this series illustrate a local Himalayan Ramayana . Their distinctive style incorporates rock formations and textiles reinterpreted from Mughal sources, probably brought to Nurpur when the Mughal emperor retreated there during the hot season.
note: The orange monkey Hanuman and the princes Lakshmana and Rama hide behind trees while Sugriva calls for Vali.

titleZh: The Heroine Who is Faithfully Loved: Madhya Svadhinapatika Nayika, from a Rasamanjari of Bhanudatta
titleEn: The Heroine Who is Faithfully Loved: Madhya Svadhinapatika Nayika, from a Rasamanjari of Bhanudatta
mediumDetail: Gum tempera, ink, and gold on paper
description: The heroine sits in front of a red cushion confiding in her friend that she feels passionate desire for her husband, but she firmly refuses his advances. Nevertheless, he continues to wait for her, remains faithful, ready to honor her. Among the different types of heroines described in the popular collection of poems called the Rasamanjari , she is projected as the supreme type.
note: The man at right nervously grasps his scarf as he respectfully approaches his lover and her companion.

titleZh: Shurpanakha demands vengeance, from the "Shangri" Ramayana
titleEn: Shurpanakha demands vengeance, from the "Shangri" Ramayana
mediumDetail: Gum tempera, ink, and gold on paper
description: In a dramatic climax, the artists introduce the demon king, Ravana (the Howler), archvillain of the Ramayana . He has 10 crowned heads and 20 arms. He grasps a different deadly weapon in each hand; they reveal his supreme powers. The demon Shurpanakha’s nose and ears are healing, but her desire for revenge is stronger than ever. She gestures emphatically at her brother Ravana, urging him to find a way to destroy Rama, perhaps by kidnapping Rama’s wife. More gold has been lavished on this painting than any other known from the “Shangri” Ramayana , suggesting that it is meant to stand out as a scene of primary importance.
note: The Ramayana of Valmiki describes Shurpanakha as hideous, misshapen, and potbellied with hair the color of copper.

titleZh: A Vignette of Life on the Frontier
titleEn: A Vignette of Life on the Frontier
mediumDetail: Folding fan; ink and color on paper
dimensions: Painting: 19 x 55 cm (7 1/2 x 21 5/8 in.); Overall with sticks: 33 x 55 cm (13 x 21 5/8 in.)
description: Jiao Bingzhen, a court painter largely active during the reign of the Kangxi Emperor, was the senior artist on this fan. Jiao painted the Manchu horse trainer and the setting into which the horse was inserted by Giuseppe Castiglione. Each artist was bonded to his own artistic tradition, while flexibly and harmoniously accommodating the others’ style. Jiao’s brushwork displays rigor and control, particularly in the twisting and turning trunk of the willow. The treatment of the figure and his clothes is an exercise in linearity. The horse trainer’s gesture and posture closely adhere to the known repertoire of the Chinese figural tradition, but the specificity supplies a sense of documentary reportage of life on the frontier. His shaved forehead and white temples identify him as a Manchu. The thick fabric of his garments was defined in a different sort of brush line than Jiao typically used for Chinese scholars or travelers. Jesuit priest Castiglione, a newcomer to China at the time this was painted, brought a sense of Western realism to the horse. Poised at a slight angle, the horse is alert, its eye gleaming. Its contours suggest the bulk of its anatomy with skilled but not overpowering modelling, and careful and subtly wrought attention to detail, such as fluttering strand of mane. Because of his ability to combine traditional Chinese painting techniques with Western methods of perspective and chiaroscuro, Castiglione went on to be the most favored and honored of the missionary artists who served the early Qing emperors. Throughout his career, in addition to imperial demands for portraits and records of court events, Castiglione continued to paint favored imperial horses. These animal subjects reflect the desire of Kangxi and his successors to celebrate their nomadic origins and to keep alive the martial prowess of the Manchu warriors in their new and sedentary world of conquered China.
note: One horseshoe is visible beneath the uplifted hoof.

titleZh: Ravana addresses Sita in the garden of Lanka, from Chapters 53 and 54 of the Aranya Kanda (Book of the Forest) of a Ramayana (Rama’s Journey)
titleEn: Ravana addresses Sita in the garden of Lanka, from Chapters 53 and 54 of the Aranya Kanda (Book of the Forest) of a Ramayana (Rama’s Journey)
mediumDetail: Gum tempera, gold, and silver on paper
description: The viewer is cut off from Lanka by the surrounding sea and the city’s golden walls in this expansive composition probably intended for courtly display This choice of perspective cleverly emphasizes the captivity of the Sita, faithful wife of the hero Rama. She kneels beneath an ashoka tree, guarded by demonesses. The princess’s abductor, the 10-headed and 20-armed demon lord of Lanka, Ravana, appears twice in the image. In the palace, he consults his council of minions. At the right, he hears Sita’s refusal to marry him. Ravana neither harms her, nor sets her free.
note: Ravana’s wives take the forms of beautiful women and fearsome demonesses.

titleZh: Thirty-Six Poetic Immortals
titleEn: Thirty-Six Poetic Immortals
mediumDetail: two-fold screen; ink, color, and gold on paper
description: Fujiwara no Kintō (996–1075), a Japanese courtier, scholar, and poet, compiled select examples by the most celebrated composers of 31-syllable poems ( waka ) from the 600s to the 1000s. Painters soon made these “thirty-six poetic immortals” a favorite subject, traditionally presenting the poets in sequential, idealized portraits paired with their poems. In this interpretation, a chronologically impossible gathering of these great talents is in progress. The screen’s composition follows one devised by design virtuoso Ogata Kōrin (1658–1716).
note: The green surface edged with stripes at the upper left of the painting represents tatami matting with a silk border.

titleZh: The Artist's Studio
titleEn: The Artist's Studio
mediumDetail: oil on copper
description: Johann Georg Platzer specialized in small, highly detailed paintings scaled for a connoisseur’s cabinet. At the center of this composition is an idealized portrait of the artist himself, clad in a fur-lined robe and holding a painting for the inspection of a visiting connoisseur. This work makes a statement about painting as a noble and intellectual pursuit, and the importance of rigorous training and practice: the artist at the easel is surrounded by a studio teeming with live models, pupils, assistants, and inspiring examples of art from earlier eras. The paintings on the wall, easel, and floor not only reference great artists of the past, but together present an allegory of the five senses.
note: Look closely—there are 12 paintings within this painting!

titleZh: View of Changmen Gate in Suzhou
titleEn: View of Changmen Gate in Suzhou
mediumDetail: Hanging scroll; multicolor woodblock print on paper, printed in two shades of black and red ink
dimensions: Image: 34.6 x 52 cm (13 5/8 x 20 1/2 in.); Overall: 110 x 66.4 cm (43 5/16 x 26 1/8 in.); Overall with knobs: 110 x 71.8 cm (43 5/16 x 28 1/4 in.)
description: This print depicts an official or imperial visit to the city of Suzhou during the Qing dynasty. Officials and residents line the streets in anticipation of a procession approaching from the left. On top of Diao bridge at the lower right, officials are wielding whips to clear the road. The emperors traditionally disembarked at the Chang Gate to visit the city on horseback, making this location a favorite pictorial theme. Written labels reveal various Suzhou businesses, such as Qianzhuang 錢莊 (private bank), Yusan hang 雨傘行 (umbrella store), and Jinjing 進京 (goods for the capital).
note: Woodblock printing in color reached a height in China in the 1600s to 1700s. The prints were executed by means of sets of separate blocks, each carved to print a different color.

titleZh: Bamboo and Rocks in Clearing Skies
titleEn: Bamboo and Rocks in Clearing Skies
mediumDetail: Two-panel folding screen; ink on paper
description: The title written on this screen corresponds to one on a design in Taiga’s Brush Methods (大雅堂画法). The concept conveyed is one of scenery and spirit refreshed by precipitation. In the screen, a rain-filled stream rushes from the mountains into a river. A village is nestled amid giant bamboo in the distance. A platform-like flat rock in the foreground invites us to step into the scene.
note: Ike Taiga ranks among the most creative painters of the Edo period: he produced over 1,000 compositions in various formats.

titleZh: Portraits of the Qianlong Emperor and His Twelve Consorts
titleEn: Portraits of the Qianlong Emperor and His Twelve Consorts
mediumDetail: Handscroll; ink and color on silk
dimensions: Overall: 53.8 x 1154.5 cm (21 3/16 x 454 1/2 in.); Painting only: 53 x 688.3 cm (20 7/8 x 271 in.)
description: This portrait shows the Qianlong emperor at 26, in the first year of his reign. His likeness is followed by portraits of the empress and eleven consorts. Their portraits document the appearances of the court women around the time when they received their respective imperial titles, which occurred at different stages of the emperor's life. The first three portraits were done by the Jesuit (Roman Catholic) missionary artist Giuseppe Castiglione, whereas the later ones were by Chinese court painters. Formal portraiture contributed to the affirmation of status and construction of role and identity. This scroll served as both familial documentation and a "mind picture" of the Qianlong emperor, suggesting that his constructed image of emperorship was inseparable from concepts of self and family. It was stored in a carved red lacquer box bearing the original painting title Mind Picture of a Well-Governed and Tranquil Reign (see CMA 1969.32 ).
note: Lingfei 令妃 (1727–1775), the first consort depicted in the maroon or “incense-colored" 香色 robe, was the mother of six of Qianlong’s children, including the future Emperor Jiaqing.

titleZh: Royal Women Celebrating Diwali
titleEn: Royal Women Celebrating Diwali
mediumDetail: gum tempera and gold on paper
description: Lined along the eaves, the top of the marble lattice railing, and the rims of the boats on the river are candles and butter lamps lit in celebration of a New Year festival. A princess on a golden armchair lights sparklers with her friends. In the boats and on the far shore men set off sparklers under the light of a magnificent firework display under the full moon. The style of this work is typical of Mughal painting from the mid-1700s, when scenes of domestic life among women of the court were a favorite subject for the imperial artists.
note: "Diwali" comes from the Sanskrit words dīpa (lamp) and āvali (rows or series).

titleZh: Pradyumna and Samvara fight with maces, from the "Large Basohli Bhagavata Purana"
titleEn: Pradyumna and Samvara fight with maces, from the "Large Basohli Bhagavata Purana"
mediumDetail: Gum tempera, ink, and gold on paper
description: Paintings from this Pahari series often place figures against boldly contrasting backgrounds. Here, the scene that takes place a moment before the prince Pradyumna’s mace, or club, vanquishes the demon Samvara is frozen in time. Years before, the demon heard a prophecy that Pradyumna would one day murder him. Hearing this, Samvara kidnapped Pradyumna as an infant and threw him into the ocean, where a fish swallowed him. The fish was caught and brought to Samvara’s kitchen, where the woman who would become his wife, Mayavati, discovered the baby still alive in its belly. Pradyumna lived to fulfill the prophecy, eventually killing the demon in this fight.
note: Pradyumna is the incarnation (avatar) of Kama, the god of erotic love.

titleZh: King Bana in his court, from an Usha-Aniruddha
titleEn: King Bana in his court, from an Usha-Aniruddha
mediumDetail: Gum tempera and ink on paper
description: This portrait of a demon king depicts him listening to the report of one of his ministers. He may be hearing the news that his daughter Usha has been secretly receiving Krishna’s grandson Aniruddha in her bedchamber. The artist has depicted Bana with his 20 arms emerging like tentacles from his body. The members of his multicolored demon court are imaginatively rendered combinations of beasts and humans. In the background, demons harass holy men by burning their huts and chasing them away from their settlements.
note: Clara Taplin Rankin, the donor of this painting, was a trustee of the CMA as well as the Musical Arts Association and the Cleveland Institute of Music.

titleZh: Print of Xu Gate and the City Moat
titleEn: Print of Xu Gate and the City Moat
mediumDetail: Multicolor woodblock print; ink and color on paper, printed in black, later hand colored, possibly in Europe
origin: Southeast China, Suzhou, Qing dynasty (1644–1911), Qianlong reign (1736–95)
description: Designed with an innovative perspective, as if the viewer is looking at the scenes through a camera lens, this round print shows the scenery and arch of Xu Gate, part of the city wall, in the west of Suzhou. The location was traditionally frequented at the lantern festival during New Year celebrations in early spring. The print thus combined multiple selling points: it could be sold to locals as New Year prints, as souvenirs to tourists, and as curious images of China to agents from overseas.
note: Woodblock printing in color reached a height in China in the 1600s to 1700s. The prints were executed by means of sets of separate blocks, each carved to print a different color.

titleZh: Basket of Plums
titleEn: Basket of Plums
mediumDetail: oil on canvas
description: During the later part of the 1700s, fruit still lifes were extremely popular, and a basket of plums was a common motif. In Vallayer's painting the details, especially the plums and the basket, emerge from deep shadows. The colors are vivid reds and violets and a sense of immediacy is invoked by the growing moss, the cakes in their crisp papers, and the glass of water with its sparkling highlights and reflections.
note: The artist painted a companion to this work—a plate of peaches and branch of cherries.

titleZh: Elizabeth Shewell West and Her Son, Raphael
titleEn: Elizabeth Shewell West and Her Son, Raphael
mediumDetail: oil on canvas
description: West was the first American artist to study in Italy, where he spent three years before permanently settling in London. He so admired the artistic ideals of the Italian Renaissance master Raphael that he named his eldest son after him, and he imitated Raphael’s celebrated Madonna of the Chair when composing this tender double portrait of his wife and child.
note: Born in colonial America, West eventually became a court painter to George III of England.

titleZh: Sleep
titleEn: Sleep
mediumDetail: oil on canvas
description: The tradition of painting nude male figures in a studio setting was the cornerstone of artistic practice, teaching artists to depict the human body in complex poses in order to create larger narratives. However, by the late 1700s, some artists began to see these studies as independent works of art. By adding the wings and the poppies, Restout transformed his study into a more specific subject, and he first exhibited the work in a privately organized exhibition in 1783 under the title of Morpheus, the god of sleep.
note: A source of inspiration for this painting was probably the Roman poet Ovid's Metamorphoses , which describes the god of sleep as living in a cave with sleep-inducing poppies at the entrance.

titleZh: The Dutton Family in the Drawing Room of Sherborne Park, Gloucestershire
titleEn: The Dutton Family in the Drawing Room of Sherborne Park, Gloucestershire
mediumDetail: oil on canvas
description: This type of picture, known as a conversation piece, was invented in England in the 1700s and popular for the informal way it represented families. A father and daughter, mother and son, are strategizing over the next hand in a game of cards. The family recently lost a loved one, so the parents are dressed in full mourning (black clothing), and the siblings in lesser mourning (mauve, white, and gray).
note: This is an idealized, not actual, room showing the sitters’ fashionable interior decorating aspirations.

titleZh: Dog with pups
titleEn: Dog with pups
mediumDetail: Gum tempera and ink on paper
origin: India, Rajasthan, Ajmer, probably Sawar school, 18th century
description: Dogs were kept in the Mughal imperial palace and attentively cared for by one keeper for every two hunting dogs. Akbar’s biography notes that the emperor liked dogs so much he imported different breeds from distant lands, and Jahangir requested English hunting dogs from the ambassador Sir Thomas Roe. The tradition of collecting and keeping dogs was continued by the succeeding emperors and vassal kings.
note: The newborn puppies are still too young to open their eyes.

titleZh: Rocky, Wooded Landscape with a Dell and Weir
titleEn: Rocky, Wooded Landscape with a Dell and Weir
mediumDetail: oil on canvas
description: In a sketchy manner, Gainsborough convincingly singled out the various elements comprising this sweeping landscape—meadow, rocks, trees—by only slightly varying colors and brushstrokes. At the same time, however, a great sense of unity prevails. Although the bulk of Gainsborough's artistic output was portraits, he insisted that landscape was his first love.
note: Gainsborough collected and was inspired by Dutch landscape painting.

titleZh: Krishna summoning the cows
titleEn: Krishna summoning the cows
mediumDetail: Gum tempera, ink, and gold on paper
dimensions: Overall: 24.3 x 27 cm (9 9/16 x 10 5/8 in.); with borders: 25.1 x 30.5 cm (9 7/8 x 12 in.)
description: As a child, Krishna grew up in a community of cow herders. He is distinguished as supernatural by his blue-colored skin and his ability to mystically draw the cows to the sound of his flute. His brother, Balarama, has white skin and wears the herdsmen’s cloak over his head and carries a red herding staff.
note: The river Jamma, also known as the Yamuna or Jumna, flows across the foreground.

titleZh: Seventy-Two Peaks Under the Blue Sky with Mount Furong
titleEn: Seventy-Two Peaks Under the Blue Sky with Mount Furong
mediumDetail: Eight-panel folding screen; ink with gold and silver foil on paper
description: The low height of this folding screen suggests its use as a partition in a small tearoom. An inscription identifies the scene as the 72-peak Heng mountain range in Hunan, China, associated with Buddhist and Daoist traditions and celebrated in poetry. Special mention in the inscription is made of Mount Furong, one of the peaks in the range. Matsumura Goshun may have drawn inspiration from his teacher, Yosa Buson (与謝蕪村) (1716–1783), whose final work depicted the same mountain range.
note: By painting on silver and gold foil, Matsumura Goshun created an alluring surface and deep space in this surprisingly spare vista.

titleZh: Cremation of the demon Putana, from a Krishna-Lila
titleEn: Cremation of the demon Putana, from a Krishna-Lila
mediumDetail: Gum tempera on paper
description: In the foreground, men of Vraj, the cowherd village where the Hindu god Krishna lived as a child, cut up the oversized corpse of the demon Putana. Already, they carry her forearms and hands to the burning pyre at the upper left. Putana arrived in the form of a wet nurse with secretly poisoned breasts. When she began to feed Krishna, he sucked the life out of her, at which point she resumed her true form. At the right, shocked cowherd women bathe baby Krishna.
note: Lila means “divine play” in Sanskrit.

titleZh: Krishna being dressed in women’s clothes for the spring festival Holi
titleEn: Krishna being dressed in women’s clothes for the spring festival Holi
mediumDetail: Ink and gum tempera on paper
description: The Hindu festival of Holi, which celebrates the arrival of spring, is a time of play that encourages reckless joy and abandon. The women cheekily dress Krishna as one of them. Radha, his beloved, takes away his crown and flute. This unfinished work reveals the process of creating an Indian painting. An experienced member of the atelier would have made the drawing and written the color notations before giving it to a colorist to paint.
note: A few preliminary patches of color in the foreground indicate the palette intended to be applied to the entire painting.
